arguments.name: Habermas cites skeptics extensively in print
arguments.conclusion: Habermas is not avoiding or hiding skeptical scholars, because his published volumes cite thousands of sources across the ideological spectrum.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Volume 3 contains roughly 8,000 footnotes and cites scholars from evangelicals to atheists.
P2: Habermas's criterion for inclusion is a terminal degree in a relevant field, regardless of the scholar's religious stance.
P3: Critics who say he refuses to name skeptics largely have not read or cited his books.

st1.quote: So, I'm not hiding in any way from names.

st2.quote: But still, there's a lot of room between 1,500 and 1,000. This book's a little under 1,000, I think. But Ben told me from his counting, Ben told me I think he said there's a little less than 8,000 footnotes in that book.

st3.quote: But Ben told me from his counting, Ben told me I think he said there's a little less than 8,000 footnotes in that book.

st4.quote: So, my overall point is once I've already done it in print, I don't think I have to call a person out.

st5.quote: So, anybody who would say, "Why don't you mention these names?" I I don't know if they're just trying to get under they're not getting under my skin that way. It doesn't bother me because I've already done the work and I've already put the sources down and I give chapter and verse for it.

st6.quote: It's my definition is if you have a terminal degree in a relevant field and I think I list six or seven relevant fields.

st7.quote: If you start accounting, the critics have gotten it. It's not Habermass mentions them one or two times and goes off on them 400 times. I mean, they get a lot of mentions. I could tell you what names to look at, too. But anybody could do a little bit of research and do it themselves.

st8.quote: And people who want to site my books can do that. But you know, you already said it. These folks largely do not site the book cuz I got a feeling am I just naive that they didn't read it and they don't know. But if there's 8,000 footnotes, I think I'm doing some citing and it's across the board. Uh evangelicals to atheists.

arguments.prior_art: none known (Habermas's own minimal-facts bibliographic corpus, e.g. The Historical Jesus, 1996)

or1.quote: So, I'm not hiding in any way from names.
or1.why: This is a bibliographic self-defense about his own four-volume work, not a restatement of any prior argument.

or2.quote: But Ben told me from his counting, Ben told me I think he said there's a little less than 8,000 footnotes in that book.
or2.why: Supplies a specific footnote count and editorial history from the volume itself.

arguments.weakest_link: The 8,000-footnote count is second-hand (Ben's count) and unverified, so the central evidence is testimonial.
arguments.develop_next: Publish an auditable index breakdown by ideological camp so the claim can be checked rather than asserted.

arguments.name: Volume 3 was an add-on research tool, not an attack
arguments.conclusion: Volume 3 was originally an add-on bibliographic catch-up volume and was not written to attack or embarrass anyone.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Habermas originally planned only three volumes and began the project to update his bibliographic follow-up after 1975.
P2: Michael Licona suggested the 1,500 pages on people's views become a fourth volume, and the publisher immediately agreed.
P3: The volume is intended to help researchers, students, and podcasters quickly locate scholarly views and quotations.

st1.quote: I didn't write it with a view to upsetting somebody. Nothing like that.

st2.quote: I was originally only going to do three volumes.

st3.quote: And Mike Lakona, there you go. Mention the name again. Michael Lona said to me, he said, "Hey, you've got these 1500 pages on people's views. I think that would interest a lot of people. Why don't you ask your publisher if they want that to be volume four?" And I did. And the head editor who's uh gone now, but the guy who's a top guy at Academics said, "Absolutely."

st4.quote: So it was an add-on volume for me to catch up and Mike said throw it in there.

st5.quote: Now, I make some personal comments about guys here and there. That's because it was my own personal document where I was going catching up from 75 and Ben typed it out.

st6.quote: I didn't write it with a view to upsetting somebody. Nothing like that.

st7.why: No kill condition or test is offered for the claim about authorial intent.

st8.quote: So, there was a lot of interest there. And so, what wasn't even going to be in the book?

or1.quote: So it was an add-on volume for me to catch up and Mike said throw it in there.
or1.why: A publication-history argument specific to this work; no prior art to restate.

or2.quote: Michael Lona said to me, he said, "Hey, you've got these 1500 pages on people's views."
or2.why: Brings the Licona/publisher origin story as new evidence.

arguments.weakest_link: Authorial intent is asserted from memory; the publisher's and Licona's independent corroboration is not produced.
arguments.develop_next: Produce the publisher's correspondence or contract record showing the four-volume decision predated any criticism.

arguments.name: Fairness challenge to critics
arguments.conclusion: Critics who complain about his citation balance should produce a comparable work with the same percentage of opposing scholars cited fairly.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Critics allege that most of his footnotes are to evangelicals or scholars friendly to evangelicals.
P2: Habermas challenges them to write a 1,000-page book citing the same percentage of skeptics as he cites evangelicals.
P3: He allows them to include a few critiques, just as he occasionally includes critiques of conservatives.

st1.quote: Here's my challenge. Okay, you write a thousandpage book and have the same percentage of evangelicals that I have of skeptics.

st2.quote: You say you don't give critiques, you sneak in a few. Okay, you can sneak in a few of evangelicals, too.

st3.quote: You know it's just human nature to cite more people that agree with you. That's that I'll just smile if you're being fair, but instead of criticizing me for, you know, how many of their names are in my index, I mean, cuz anybody can go through, if they want to, they don't have to go to the index.

st4.quote: I want to see who wears the skeptical work that cites as many of the conservatives nicely without same thing you critique me for without giving critiques.

st5.quote: I'm going to give you a little bit more room because you're not an evangelical.

st6.quote: But I want you to have the same percentage of treating evangelicals nicely and citing them in your work as of yours.

st7.quote: Here's my challenge. Okay, you write a thousandpage book and have the same percentage of evangelicals that I have of skeptics.

st8.why: Only one line of support (the symmetry challenge) is offered.

or1.quote: Here's my challenge. Okay, you write a thousandpage book and have the same percentage of evangelicals that I have of skeptics.
or1.why: A tu quoque symmetry challenge, not a restatement of a prior argument.

or2.quote: I know it's just human nature to cite more people that agree with you.
or2.why: Adds a psychological concession as support, but little new data.

arguments.weakest_link: The challenge shifts the burden of proof rather than answering whether the citation balance is actually fair.
arguments.develop_next: Supply the actual percentage breakdown of his own footnotes so the symmetry claim is measurable.

arguments.name: No numerical threshold for 'highly evidenced'
arguments.conclusion: The first minimal-facts criterion, 'highly evidenced,' should not be reduced to a fixed percentage; it is better understood through categories of strong historical evidence.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Habermas has never counted scholars or assigned a percentage threshold except in his empty-tomb study.
P2: He measures evidence by categories such as multiple attestation, eyewitness testimony, and early sources.
P3: If he gave a number such as 80%, critics would misrepresent it as an arbitrary criterion.

st1.quote: But I do not have a certain threshold that they have to have to meet.

st2.quote: I'd say if I have multiple attestation, eyewitness and early sources, that's not a list of names. That's a list of categories.

st3.quote: When we do criteria we many many commentators have said that multiple attestation is the best evidence for documents multiple attestation.

st4.quote: So, after a while, I don't measure by how many do I have. I measure by do I have a fair number of multiple attestation.

st5.quote: But somebody will say that was the number he gave. And uh I'm not doing that at all.

st6.quote: And I think those categories to have several of those makes a strong argument.

st7.quote: If I said, "Well, Dale, you give uh 51. I'd like at least 80." They're going to go, "See, he means 80."

st8.quote: I'd say if I have multiple attestation, eyewitness and early sources, that's not a list of names. That's a list of categories. And I think those categories to have several of those makes a strong argument.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, minimal facts criteria (The Historical Jesus, 1996)

or1.quote: But I do not have a certain threshold that they have to have to meet.
or1.why: A clarification/variant of his own established criterion rather than a new argument.

or2.quote: If you have 20 good evidences for the empty tomb which I listed I they're there in a volume one as I recall.
or2.why: Reuses his own prior list of 20 evidences as illustration.

arguments.weakest_link: Refusing any quantitative threshold leaves 'highly evidenced' vague and hard to test.
arguments.develop_next: State an explicit decision rule (e.g., multiple independent early sources) that distinguishes 'highly evidenced' from other facts.

arguments.name: Non-evangelical scholars support the minimal facts
arguments.conclusion: The minimal facts are strongly supported even by non-evangelical and skeptical scholars, which strengthens the case that they are not merely Christian bias.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: James D. G. Dunn, a non-evangelical, holds that the resurrection preaching and creedal statements may go back within months of the crucifixion.
P2: Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, says the preaching of the resurrection began immediately.
P3: Bart Ehrman concedes it is a historical fact that the disciples thought they saw the risen Jesus.
P4: Dale Allison says the minimal facts approach is the best apologetical argument and that his skeptical approach does not deny any of the minimal facts.

st1.quote: I think if I have non-eangelicals saying those things, that that interests me.

st2.quote: The German scholar Garrett Ludman Jesus seminar me remember Ludman said the preaching of the resurrection. Now that's one of the minimal facts. The preaching began immediately.

st3.quote: Quote, I think the minimal facts approach is the best of the apologetical arguments. Gary is right to pay attention to that. My skeptical approach doesn't deny any of the minimal facts. Dale Allison, who I've heard called in a couple contexts now, one of the three top New Testament guys in the world.

st4.quote: And Jimmy Dunn, there's very few people better. He he seems like he's it sounds like he's saying the original creedle statements could have come that first year.

st5.quote: Now, he does say in one place in one of his books, he says, "I'm not a skeptic." But here he says, "My skeptical approach." So, at least his method.

st6.quote: I think if Dale is one of the top few, and he's quote unquote skeptical, and he doesn't deny any of them, and he thinks it's the best argument.

st7.quote: I can find my six facts over and over and over and over and over. And James DG Dunn.

st8.quote: The German scholar Garrett Ludman Jesus seminar me remember Ludman said the preaching of the resurrection. Now that's one of the minimal facts. The preaching began immediately.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas & Michael Licona, The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus, 2004

or1.quote: I think if I have non-eangelicals saying those things, that that interests me.
or1.why: A variant of the standard minimal-facts consensus argument, with updated names and quotes.

or2.quote: Quote, I think the minimal facts approach is the best of the apologetical arguments. Gary is right to pay attention to that. My skeptical approach doesn't deny any of the minimal facts.
or2.why: Adds fresh Allison, Dunn, Lüdemann and Ehrman quotations not in the 2004 case.

arguments.weakest_link: The inference from 'these scholars grant the facts' to 'the facts are not Christian bias' depends on the sample being representative, which is not shown.
arguments.develop_next: Give a systematic count of non-evangelical scholars on each minimal fact rather than a handful of named quotations.

arguments.name: Scholarly consensus alone is not sufficient
arguments.conclusion: The scholarly-consensus criterion is not by itself sufficient for rational belief; the evidence criterion is far more important.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Habermas says criterion one is by far the more important of the two, perhaps 85-90% of the case.
P2: If the second criterion disappeared, one would be no worse off than other ancient historians.
P3: Scholarly consensus can be wrong if it is based on bias or social pressure.

st1.quote: I think number one is so far ahead of number two that I think if number two disappears no biggie.

st2.quote: I'd say number one is I got to think about this. This sounds stupid for me to say that in my mind number one would be 90 or 85% of the game.

st3.quote: I'll say, "What happens if we wake up one morning, there's a big uprising, and 10% of scholars admit this admit these data?" I say, "Okay, if there's a time when I have to drop my second criterion, how bad am I off?" No worse off than uh other ancient histo ancient historians.

st4.quote: I think number one is so far ahead of number two that I think if number two disappears no biggie.

st5.quote: I even I would admit scholarly cons just the scholarly consensus alone they're often wrong. So it has to be a proper consensus. You know one that's not based on bias or some kind of social or political pressure or something like that.

st6.quote: But if I'm going to make it an argument at all, it's going to be down my line.

st7.quote: I'll say, "What happens if we wake up one morning, there's a big uprising, and 10% of scholars admit this admit these data?"

st8.quote: If all you have are the data, that's mostly what you want.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas & Michael Licona, The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus, 2004 (minimal-facts two criteria)

or1.quote: I think number one is so far ahead of number two that I think if number two disappears no biggie.
or1.why: A refinement of his own two-criteria framework rather than a new argument.

or2.quote: I'd say number one is I got to think about this. This sounds stupid for me to say that in my mind number one would be 90 or 85% of the game.
or2.why: Adds a rough weighting estimate, though admittedly unbacked.

arguments.weakest_link: The 85-90% weighting for the evidence criterion is admitted to be a guess with no count behind it.
arguments.develop_next: Show that dropping the consensus criterion really leaves one no worse off than other ancient historians by a concrete comparative case study.
